study_sample_descriptor.country_specify: 16 R&D labs across the United States (4 labs), Europe (10 labs), and Asia (2 labs)
study_sample_descriptor.sample_quote: Our predictions were tested using original data collected in the R&D division of a large multinational and multidivisional high-tech company. In particular, we collected questionnaire and archival data on 276 respondents who were identified by senior management as “all the employees with active research and development duties in the R&D division.” These researchers were spread over 16 labs around the world: 4 in the United States, 10 in Europe, and 2 in Asia. The average lab consisted of 25 individuals. The population studied comprised mostly males (90%) who were highly educated (9 percent had Ph.D.s; 78 percent, master’s degree; and 13 percent, college degrees or less) and had relatively low organizational seniority (average tenure, 5.2 years). The network data consisted of information on self-reported knowledge-sharing ties collected through a sociometric instrument. The survey yielded a response rate of about 89 percent (245 actual respondents out of 276 potential respondents).

boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network survey of confirmed reciprocal knowledge-sharing ties (rated 1 = seldom to 5 = very frequently, 0 = n/a) used to compute the E-I index (ranging from -1 to +1) across vs. within R&D labs.
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: The network data were derived from two network survey questions: (1) “Please indicate how often you generally go to this person for information or knowledge on work-related topics” and (2) “Please indicate how often this person generally comes to you for information or knowledge on work-related topics” (for both questions, the response scale ranged from 1, “seldom,” to 5, “very frequently”). In general, the E-I index is a measure of the extent to which a party’s ties form a bridge across some organizational or social divide (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988). For example, the variable “bridging direct raw ties” represents the value on the E-I index calculated for a individual based on the set of confirmed ties for that individual.
boundary_spanning_measures.items_quote: The E-I index ranges from -1 (when all ties to/from i are internal ties) to +1 (when all ties to/from i are external or bridging ties).

boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network survey of confirmed reciprocal weak knowledge-sharing ties (average tie strength <= 3.5 on 1-5 scale) used to compute the E-I index (ranging from -1 to +1) across vs. within R&D labs.
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: As stated above, we measured the raw ties on a 1–5 scale. We categorized ties as strong or weak using the dichotomy 4 and above versus 3.5 and below (recall that confirmed ties RV are the average of the two individuals’ responses, hence the possible fractional values). Strong ties, then, were defined as any tie whose value RV was greater than or equal to 4. Weak ties were the remaining ones—that is, ties whose value RV was smaller than or equal to 3.5. In general, the E-I index is a measure of the extent to which a party’s ties form a bridge across some organizational or social divide (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988).
boundary_spanning_measures.items_quote: Specifically, in model 6 we consider bridging weak ties and in model 7 we consider bridging strong ties.

boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network survey of confirmed reciprocal strong knowledge-sharing ties (average tie strength >= 4 on 1-5 scale) used to compute the E-I index (ranging from -1 to +1) across vs. within R&D labs.

boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network survey of confirmed reciprocal non-Simmelian knowledge-sharing ties (ties not embedded in cliques) used to compute the E-I index (ranging from -1 to +1) across vs. within R&D labs.
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: We used the direct formulation provided by Krackhardt (1998), according to which a tie from i to j (that is, Ri, j = 1) is Simmelian if and only if it satisfies the following two conditions: Rj, i = 1 (1) and there exists k such that Ri, k = Rk, i = Rj, k = Rk, j = 1. (2) A non-Simmelian tie from i to j is any tie that does not satisfy these conditions for being Simmelian. In general, the E-I index is a measure of the extent to which a party’s ties form a bridge across some organizational or social divide (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988).
boundary_spanning_measures.items_quote: All the variables beginning “bridging” refer to the E-I index calculations for the different types of ties.

boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network survey of confirmed reciprocal Simmelian knowledge-sharing ties (ties embedded in cliques with at least one common third party) used to compute the E-I index (ranging from -1 to +1) across vs. within R&D labs.
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: Simmelian ties, as stated earlier and as described in Krackhardt (1998, 1999) and discussed in detail in Dekker (2006), are defined as ties embedded in cliques. In general, the E-I index is a measure of the extent to which a party’s ties form a bridge across some organizational or social divide (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988). “Bridging Simmelian ties” represents the E-I index calculated on the set of Simmelian ties for that individual, and so forth.
boundary_spanning_measures.items_quote: The E-I index ranges from -1 (when all ties to/from i are internal ties) to +1 (when all ties to/from i are external or bridging ties).

boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network survey of confirmed weak non-Simmelian knowledge-sharing ties used to compute the E-I index (ranging from -1 to +1) across vs. within R&D labs.
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: In general, the E-I index is a measure of the extent to which a party’s ties form a bridge across some organizational or social divide (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988). In particular, by taking tie strength into account, we defined four mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories of network ties and evaluated the extent to which they bridged organizational boundaries by computing the E-I index for each. The four categories were (1) weak non-Simmelian ties, (2) strong non-Simmelian ties, (3) weak Simmelian ties, and (4) strong Simmelian ties.
boundary_spanning_measures.items_quote: The E-I index ranges from -1 (when all ties to/from i are internal ties) to +1 (when all ties to/from i are external or bridging ties).

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Archival count of patent applications filed by the individual across 18 monthly company R&D reports (6 months before and 12 months after social network data collection).
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: number of patents filed by individuals in the sample
non_bs_measures.source_quote: Our dependent variable was the number of patents filed by individuals in the sample. The company made patent data available in the form of monthly R&D reports used to assess and reward individual performance. For each of the 16 labs studied, the company made available a total of 18 monthly reports, 6 before and 12 after the collection of social network data. Cross-examination of all reports allowed us to identify patent applications filed by respondents in our sample.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: Indeed, it was the number of patent applications reported in the monthly report that formed the basis for performance review and promotion decisions.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network count of confirmed strong knowledge-sharing ties (average tie value >= 4 on a 1-5 scale).
non_bs_measures.source_quote: From these raw data represented as Vs, we created a network relation of “confirmed” ties, RVi, j (Carley & Krackhardt, 1996). As stated above, we measured the raw ties on a 1–5 scale. We categorized ties as strong or weak using the dichotomy 4 and above versus 3.5 and below (recall that confirmed ties RV are the average of the two individuals’ responses, hence the possible fractional values). Strong ties, then, were defined as any tie whose value RV was greater than or equal to 4.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: Model 4 tests for the main effect of having a network composed primarily of strong ties.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Organizational job grade of researchers (questionnaire and archival data).
non_bs_measures.source_quote: We also controlled for the level of education, seniority, and organizational job grade of researchers as a possible indicator of their ability and experience.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: We also controlled for the level of education, seniority, and organizational job grade of researchers as a possible indicator of their ability and experience.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network measure of structural holes / constraint (Burt, 1992: 55).
non_bs_measures.source_quote: Past research has used the presence of structural holes (or its counterpart, constraint) as a measure of many of the concepts in this study, including bridging, informational advantages, and closure. To make sure that our results were not simply a reflection of the effects of this construct, we included the existence of structural holes (Burt, 1992: 55) as a control in our models.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: To make sure that our results were not simply a reflection of the effects of this construct, we included the existence of structural holes (Burt, 1992: 55) as a control in our models.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Dummy variable identifying whether the respondent is a laboratory head.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: dummy variable that identified the lab heads in our sample
non_bs_measures.source_quote: Another possible confound was the fact that often lab heads are registered as filing patents developed by researchers in their labs. To control for this, we introduced a dummy variable that identified the lab heads in our sample.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: To control for this, we introduced a dummy variable that identified the lab heads in our sample.

non_bs_measures.table_anchor_name: Degree of alters located outside ego’s lab
non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network measure of the degree centrality (number of direct ties) of the alters located in other labs to which ego was connected.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: degree centrality of the alters located in other labs to which each ego was connected
non_bs_measures.source_quote: One last set of control variables allowed us to take into account individuals’ relational features, such as the size of their networks (measured as number of ties), the degree centrality of the alters located in other labs to which each ego was connected, structural holes, and laboratory size (the number of people in ego’s lab). Similarly, by controlling for the degree centrality of alters located in other labs to which an ego is connected, we addressed the alternative explanation that variation in individuals’ innovativeness was a result of their having bridging ties to individuals who themselves had very large networks in their own labs.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: Degree centrality is given by the number of direct ties a given node has.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Archival dummy variable from USPTO database coded 1 if respondent had filed at least one patent in the 3 years before the 18-month study window, and 0 otherwise.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: dummy variable measuring their prior patenting experience
non_bs_measures.source_quote: For instance, to account for individuals’ idiosyncratic ability to generate patents, we created a dummy variable measuring their prior patenting experience. This variable was coded 1 if a respondent had filed at least one patent in the three years before the 18 months considered in the study, and 0 otherwise. We obtained this information by searching the USPTO database for all the patents filed by respondents in our sample in the three years before our 18-month window.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: This variable was coded 1 if a respondent had filed at least one patent in the three years before the 18 months considered in the study, and 0 otherwise.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Sociometric network size measured as total number of confirmed knowledge-sharing ties.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: size of their networks (measured as number of ties)
non_bs_measures.source_quote: One last set of control variables allowed us to take into account individuals’ relational features, such as the size of their networks (measured as number of ties), the degree centrality of the alters located in other labs to which each ego was connected, structural holes, and laboratory size (the number of people in ego’s lab). Controlling for network size helped to rule out the possible alternative explanation that it was the sheer number of knowledge-sharing ties that predicted variation in individuals’ innovativeness.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: Controlling for network size helped to rule out the possible alternative explanation that it was the sheer number of knowledge-sharing ties that predicted variation in individuals’ innovativeness.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Archival count of the number of scientists/people in ego's R&D laboratory.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: laboratory size (the number of people in ego’s lab)
non_bs_measures.source_quote: One last set of control variables allowed us to take into account individuals’ relational features, such as the size of their networks (measured as number of ties), the degree centrality of the alters located in other labs to which each ego was connected, structural holes, and laboratory size (the number of people in ego’s lab). And finally, it is possible that the number of scientists at a lab, or lab size, could affect both the productivity of its members as well as opportunities for interaction. Therefore, we also controlled for lab size in the models.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: And finally, it is possible that the number of scientists at a lab, or lab size, could affect both the productivity of its members as well as opportunities for interaction.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Mean of 4 items measuring scientific external knowledge sourced from outside the organization.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: Scientific external knowledge was also defined by four items
non_bs_measures.source_quote: For this reason, we decided to control in our models for the type and amount of knowledge sourced from outside the organization. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation on eight different sources of external knowledge allowed us to identify two distinct factors: scientific external knowledge and industrial external knowledge. Scientific external knowledge was also defined by four items; the alpha coefficient was .81, and the first principal component from a factor analysis of the items explained 58.4 percent of the variance. The indicators for the sources of each form of external knowledge were the means of the respective four items.
non_bs_measures.items_quote: Scientific external knowledge was also defined by four items; the alpha coefficient was .81, and the first principal component from a factor analysis of the items explained 58.4 percent of the variance.

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: Mean of 4 items measuring industrial external knowledge sourced from outside the organization.
non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: Industrial external knowledge was defined by four items
non_bs_measures.source_quote: For this reason, we decided to control in our models for the type and amount of knowledge sourced from outside the organization. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation on eight different sources of external knowledge allowed us to identify two distinct factors: scientific external knowledge and industrial external knowledge. Industrial external knowledge was defined by four items with a Cronbach’s coefficient alpha of .76 and a first principal component explaining 63.2 percent of the variance. The indicators for the sources of each form of external knowledge were the means of the respective four items.
